demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Amara had not intended to look away from the load distribution schedule when the clipboard slipped from her hands. It was a Tuesday, the kind of humid Georgia afternoon that made the steel frame of the new municipal center feel like an oven. She had bent to retrieve it, her boot catching on a frayed nylon strap she had failed to notice during her morning walk-through. The strap, already fatigued from days of tension, gave way with a sharp crack. A steel I-beam, resting on the temporary rigging, shifted. She heard the metal groan before she saw it fall, a sound that still sometimes echoed in the quiet of her drafting room three years later. When she looked up, a site foreman was on the ground, his leg pinned beneath the shifting weight, blood already soaking into the concrete dust. In the months that followed, Amara found herself unable to deliberately summon the details of that afternoon. The memory refused to stay in her conscious grasp, slipping away like water through her fingers whenever she tried to pin it down. Yet when it returned, it brought with it the sharp, metallic taste of dried blood and the acrid scent of crushed drywall that had settled in her mouth. She would also hear the foreman's choked breath and the subsequent radio chatter from the site monitors, crackling through the back of her mind. At the architectural firm on Peachtree Street, ordinary office routines had become landscapes of quiet hazards. When the telephone rang beside her desk, it acted as a trigger, sending a jolt through her nervous system before her mind could confirm the line was simply idle. She caught herself staring at a rendered façade, the blue lines of a structural grid blurring into gray static as her focus fractured. Before submitting any set of plans, Amara would run her fingers along the binding three times and whisper a silent count to ensure no harm would follow. She told herself that the foreman had walked out with crutches, that others in her position would have lost a hand or a leg. But the rumination continued alongside it. She replayed the morning walk-through over and over, certain that a single overlooked measurement, a half-second delay in her own attention, was the reason the strap had snapped. People in the firm still addressed her by her first name, but Amara felt herself drifting into a quiet separation from them. She declined the Friday site visits and stopped attending the monthly design critiques, telling herself she was simply managing her workload. In reality, she felt fundamentally different from the colleagues who laughed in the breakroom and moved through their days without flinching at the sudden ring of a cell phone. When she looked in the mirror while preparing for bed, she barely recognized the woman staring back. The architect who once commanded site walks with a steady voice and a sharp eye for detail was gone, replaced by someone who checked every doorway twice. She was certain that anyone else would have handled the rigging schedule differently, would have been in a position to make a mistake like hers at all. For months, she carried this isolation in her chest, a heavy, private weight that no amount of reassurance from her husband or the evening walks they used to take could lift. What finally brought her through the clinic doors was not a single crisis, but the slow realization that she was no longer able to stand at her drafting table without her hands shaking. She sat in the therapist's office now, her pen tucked away, not because she had solved the problem, but because she was desperate to remember how to breathe while she worked. She hoped, more than anything, to find a way to exist in her own life again without bracing for the next collapse.
